overview: Vector Limited owns and operates the regulated electricity distribution network covering Auckland (from Wellsford to central Papakura, plus Waiheke and Great Barrier Islands) and the Auckland gas distribution network, serving over 640,000 electricity and ~120,000 gas connections. The company has transformed its portfolio over FY2023-FY2024, selling its metering business (retaining a 50% stake in the renamed Bluecurrent joint venture with QIC) and its natural gas trading business (Ongas/Liquigas), leaving a simplified structure of regulated electricity distribution, regulated gas distribution, and a smaller 'Other' segment (Vector Technology Solutions, HRV, Vector Fibre). Vector is majority-owned (75.1%) by Entrust, a community trust that distributes an annual cash dividend to ~370,000+ Auckland electricity consumer beneficiaries, with the balance of shares NZX-listed and freely traded (ticker VCT).

business_model.summary: Vector is fundamentally a regulated-asset-base (RAB) utility: it earns revenue set under the Commerce Commission's Default Price-Quality Path (DPP) framework for electricity distribution, reset every five years (current period DPP4, effective 1 April 2025 to 31 March 2030), which determines allowable revenue based on the regulatory asset base, an allowed rate of return (WACC, currently favourable given the higher interest rate environment baked into DPP4), depreciation, and pass-through costs (e.g. Transpower transmission charges). Gas distribution operates under a similar but separate DPQP regime. Revenue is highly recurring and monopoly-protected (network access charges paid by all retailers/consumers on the network) but growth requires capital investment; capital contributions from customers for new connections partly offset gross capex. The 'Other' segment (Vector Technology Solutions/VTS, HRV, Vector Fibre, and 50%-owned Bluecurrent JV) contributes a much smaller, less regulated, and currently loss-making-to-marginal earnings stream, though Bluecurrent distributions ($55m in FY26) are growing.

revenue_streams.name: Electricity distribution (Adjusted EBITDA)
revenue_streams.notes: FY26: $440m adjusted EBITDA (+25% YoY) on revenue growth driven by the DPP4 reset (effective 1 April 2025) which recognises higher allowable returns from higher interest rates/inflation and pass-through of Transpower transmission cost increases. 642,134 total connections (+1.6% YoY).

revenue_streams.name: Gas distribution (Adjusted EBITDA)
revenue_streams.notes: FY26: $47m adjusted EBITDA (flat YoY). Volumes declining (11.7PJ, -1.7% YoY in FY26; -4.5% in H1FY26) as the sector transitions away from gas; new connections slowing sharply (720 in FY26 vs 1,300 in FY25). A structurally declining but still regulated, cash-generative business.

revenue_streams.name: Other (VTS, HRV, Vector Fibre, Bluecurrent JV share)
revenue_streams.notes: Small, non-reportable segment; often near break-even to slightly negative on an adjusted EBITDA basis in recent periods. Bluecurrent (50% JV with QIC, advanced metering) is cash-flow positive and paying growing distributions ($55m FY26) but reports a net loss at the NPAT line from debt-funded growth, meter depreciation and contract amortisation, which flows through Vector's 'share of associates' P&L line.

business_model.customer_type: Effectively B2B2C — Vector's direct customers are electricity and gas retailers who use its distribution network to reach end consumers; ultimate economic bearers of network charges are Auckland households and businesses. Also has direct B2B/B2C exposure through Vector Technology Solutions, HRV (home ventilation), and Vector Fibre.
business_model.geographic_mix: 100% Auckland region for the core regulated networks (electricity: Wellsford to central Papakura plus islands; gas: wider Auckland region). Bluecurrent JV also operates metering assets in Australia.

main_competitors: No direct competitor for the core Auckland electricity/gas distribution networks — these are regulated natural-monopoly infrastructure with no realistic prospect of a parallel network being built

Other NZ regulated electricity distribution businesses (EDBs) as regulatory/political benchmarks rather than direct competitors: Powerco, Orion, Wellington Electricity, Unison, Aurora Energy, Northpower
Bluecurrent JV competes with other advanced metering providers (e.g. Intellihub) in NZ and Australia
Vector Technology Solutions/cyber security services competes with other technology/managed-services vendors for electricity distribution business clients
HRV competes in the home ventilation/heat pump market against other home comfort providers
competitive_position.market_position: Sole regulated distributor for the Auckland electricity and gas networks — a structural, government-sanctioned monopoly rather than a market-share position. Vector is one of the largest EDBs in New Zealand by regulated asset base and connection count, reflecting Auckland's status as NZ's largest city.

moat_factors.description: Electricity and gas distribution networks are licensed, capital-intensive natural monopolies; duplicating physical network infrastructure in Auckland is not economically or practically feasible. Revenue is protected by the Commerce Commission's price-quality regulation, which guarantees a regulated return on the asset base rather than exposing Vector to market competition for volume.

moat_factors.factor: Regulated asset base and rate-of-return mechanism
moat_factors.description: The DPP framework provides revenue certainty over five-year cycles once set. The current DPP4 (1 April 2025 - 31 March 2030) reset delivered materially higher allowable revenue reflecting the current higher interest rate/inflation environment, directly lifting adjusted EBITDA (+$88m in FY26 electricity EBITDA growth attributed largely to the reset).

As Auckland is NZ's largest and fastest-growing city, Vector benefits from structural connection growth (new subdivisions, population growth, electrification of transport/industry, data centre demand) that smaller regional EDBs do not enjoy to the same degree.

75.1% ownership by Entrust (a permanent community trust structure) provides long-term ownership stability and insulates Vector from hostile takeover or short-term activist pressure, but also means governance and capital allocation (e.g. dividend policy) must balance Entrust beneficiary cash distributions against network investment needs.

weaknesses: Revenue and earnings are ultimately capped by the Commerce Commission regulatory settings, not organic market growth or pricing power — upside from strong Auckland growth can be partially clawed back at the next reset

No genuine diversification: with metering and gas trading sold, Vector is now overwhelmingly a single-city (Auckland), single-regulator earnings stream, concentrating regulatory and Auckland-specific (e.g. natural disaster, storm/cyclone) risk
Sub-scale non-regulated 'Other' segment (VTS/HRV/Fibre) has not yet demonstrated it can be a meaningful earnings contributor and has recently been shrinking/loss-making
Structural capex intensity means the business is persistently a net cash consumer before financing, requiring ongoing access to debt (and potentially equity) markets on reasonable terms

Political/public sentiment risk around network reliability (storm outages, e.g. Auckland Anniversary floods/Cyclone Gabrielle in 2023) and rising consumer electricity bills, given Vector's charges flow through to household power bills at a time of cost-of-living pressure

growth_drivers: Auckland population and economic growth driving new electricity and gas connections (642,134 electricity connections at FY26, +1.6% YoY; ~13,000 new connections added in FY26)

Electrification of transport (EVs) and industry: 48,434+ EVs registered in Auckland as of FY24 and rising; Vector is investing in smart/managed EV charging (Dynamic Operating Envelope) to defer costly network reinforcement

Data centre demand: Vector expects up to 500MW of new demand from data centres connecting to the Auckland network over the next five years — a large, concentrated new load category requiring significant capex but also revenue growth

Long-term Asset Management Plan (AMP26): a flagged $10 billion, 20-year investment programme for the Auckland electricity network (c.$4.5bn invested over the past decade, a further $5.4bn planned FY2026-FY2036), roughly half earmarked for growth connections (new homes, businesses, large loads like data centres) and half for renewal/resilience

DPP4 regulatory reset (effective 1 April 2025, 5-year term to March 2030) locking in higher allowable returns reflecting the current higher interest-rate and inflation environment, plus full pass-through of Transpower transmission cost increases
Growing Bluecurrent (50% JV, advanced metering data services) distributions as the metering business scales in NZ and Australia ($55m distribution received in FY26, up from ~$52m in FY25)

Vector Technology Solutions: cyber security and digital/data services offered to other NZ electricity distribution businesses (six external EDB customers as at FY2024) — an early-stage adjacent growth avenue leveraging Vector's networks expertise

Distributed energy resources (solar, batteries) and demand orchestration (Symphony strategy) creating new network services and potentially deferring/reducing the capital intensity of meeting peak demand growth

business.risk: Network reliability and resilience under extreme weather
business.description: Auckland is exposed to increasingly severe storm events (e.g. the 2023 Auckland Anniversary floods and Cyclone Gabrielle); Vector has previously breached extreme-event outage quality standards (Warkworth area, FY24). Major outage events generate significant public and political scrutiny, potential compensation/penalty exposure, and reputational damage, while resilience capex often competes with growth capex for funding priority.

business.risk: Concentration in a single regulated network/single city
business.description: With metering and gas trading divested, virtually all of Vector's earnings now derive from the Auckland electricity (and to a lesser extent gas) distribution networks. There is no geographic or regulatory diversification to offset an adverse outcome from any single Commerce Commission decision or Auckland-specific event.

Gas connection growth has turned negative to flat (new connections down from 1,300 in FY25 to 720 in FY26; volumes down 1.7-4.5% YoY across recent periods) as electrification and decarbonisation reduce reliance on gas. While currently still profitable and regulated, the segment's terminal value and future regulatory treatment (e.g. asset stranding, accelerated depreciation) are uncertain over a multi-decade horizon; Vector already recorded a $60m gas distribution impairment in FY2024.

The 50%-owned Bluecurrent JV reported a net loss (NPAT contribution of -$24.9m in FY2024) despite being cash-flow positive, driven by debt-funded growth and meter depreciation/contract amortisation. Continued reliance on debt funding for JV growth could pressure Vector's share of associate earnings and carrying value ($594m as at H1FY26) if the metering market becomes more competitive or growth slows.

financial.risk: Structural capex-funding gap requiring continuous debt issuance
financial.description: Gross capex has structurally and materially exceeded operating cash flow for years, and management has now guided record capex of $605-635m for FY2027 (up from $544m in FY2026) as part of a flagged $5.4bn network investment programme through FY2036. This capex supercycle must be funded predominantly by new debt (net capex was $353m in FY26, +36% YoY), progressively increasing economic net debt (NZ$2.28bn at FY26, up from NZ$2.16bn a year earlier) and gearing (39% at FY26, though well down from the 57-59% range of FY2021-22 following metering/gas trading sale proceeds).

financial.risk: Interest rate exposure on a large and growing debt book
financial.description: With economic net debt of ~$2.28bn (rising toward $2.5bn+ implied by capex guidance) and finance costs a material P&L line, Vector is directly exposed to NZ and offshore interest rate movements on both floating and refinanced fixed-rate debt. Ironically, the current DPP4 regulatory settings reward Vector with a higher allowed return specifically because of the elevated interest rate environment — creating a partial (but not perfect or contemporaneous) natural hedge between funding cost and allowed revenue.

financial.risk: Dividend policy relinked to cash flow (Feb 2025) constrains payout growth
financial.description: The Board revised the dividend policy in February 2025 to link distributions to cash flow generation across the five-year DPP regulatory cycle rather than a fixed per-share growth trajectory. While intended to align payouts with actual cash generation given the capex supercycle, this could mean flatter or less predictable dividend growth for minority shareholders than under the prior policy, particularly in years of peak capex.

Vector carries an S&P long-term credit rating of BBB+ (outlook has moved between stable and positive across 2024-2026 commentary). Maintaining investment-grade metrics is important given reliance on wholesale bond and USPP markets to fund the capex programme; a ratings downgrade would raise funding costs at exactly the point capex needs are increasing.

regulatory.risk: Five-yearly DPP reset risk (next reset ~2030 for electricity)
regulatory.description: Nearly all of Vector's core earnings power is determined by the Commerce Commission's periodic Default Price-Quality Path resets. While the current DPP4 (1 April 2025 - 31 March 2030) is favourable, reflecting higher allowed returns from elevated interest rates and inflation, this represents a structural risk that could reverse at the next reset if interest rates or the Commission's methodology change, or if the Commission tightens allowed returns/quality standards in response to affordability or reliability pressures.

regulatory.risk: Consumer affordability and political pressure on network charges
regulatory.description: Vector's own management has publicly called for wider energy market/regulatory reform, citing cost-of-living pressures on customers from rising lines charges (which the Commission has agreed to 'smooth' over the DPP4 period rather than allow one-off shocks). Sustained public and political pressure over electricity affordability could result in tighter future regulatory settings or ad hoc government intervention.

regulatory.risk: Gas distribution regulatory treatment amid energy transition
regulatory.description: As NZ and Auckland decarbonise, future gas distribution price-quality regulation could increasingly reflect stranded-asset risk, accelerated depreciation allowances, or reduced allowed returns, as regulators and policymakers grapple with a shrinking customer base funding a fixed network.

regulatory.risk: EV charging and distributed energy resource standards
regulatory.description: Vector has lobbied for mandated 'smart' EV charging standards to avoid costly reactive network reinforcement; failure to secure timely regulatory support for demand orchestration could force more expensive, less efficient capital investment to manage electrification-driven peak demand.

macro.risk: NZ interest rate and monetary policy environment
macro.description: As a heavily debt-funded, capital-intensive utility, Vector's funding costs move with NZ (and to an extent global) interest rates. The DPP4 settings provide a partial offsetting mechanism (higher allowed returns when rates/inflation are elevated) but with a lag, since allowed WACC is set at the start of each five-year period rather than continuously updated.

macro.risk: Auckland/NZ economic growth and construction cost inflation
macro.description: Vector's growth capex and connection growth are directly tied to Auckland's population and construction activity; a prolonged NZ economic downturn or construction sector slowdown would reduce new-connection growth and capital contribution revenue. Simultaneously, general cost inflation in materials, contractor labour, and specialist engineering skills increases the cost of delivering the capex programme.

The flagged 500MW of prospective data centre demand over five years is a major driver behind Vector's elevated capex guidance, but individual data centre projects can be delayed, downsized, or relocated based on global capital allocation decisions by hyperscalers, creating a risk that Vector over- or under-invests relative to actual realised demand.

execution.description: Long-serving CEO Simon Mackenzie (in the role since 2008) stepped down in 2025 after leading the metering and gas trading divestitures and the Symphony strategy; Chris Blenkiron (previously CEO of Rio Tinto's Tiwai smelter, with a manufacturing/building-products background rather than utilities/networks) commenced as Group CEO in December 2025. A strategic review under the new CEO, with outcomes to be detailed at the September 2026 shareholder meeting, introduces some uncertainty as to whether capital allocation priorities, the pace of the AMP26 investment programme, or the 'Other' segment portfolio (VTS/HRV/Fibre) could change.

execution.risk: Delivering a record, escalating capex programme
execution.description: Guided gross capex of $605-635m for FY2027 (a new record, up from $544m in FY2026, which was itself up 16% YoY) requires Vector to significantly scale contractor capacity, project management, and supply chains simultaneously, in a tight NZ construction/engineering labour market, while maintaining service reliability and cost discipline that ultimately determine future regulatory outcomes and consumer/political goodwill.

macro_factors.industry_outlook: NZ electricity distribution is a structurally growing but heavily regulated sector, driven by decarbonisation/electrification (EVs, industrial electrification), Auckland-specific population growth, and a new wave of large-load demand from data centres. Regulatory settings (Commerce Commission DPPs) are currently constructive for distribution businesses given the higher-rate environment baked into DPP4, but the sector faces persistent political and consumer scrutiny over electricity affordability. Gas distribution is in slow structural decline nationally as decarbonisation policy discourages new gas connections.
macro_factors.cyclicality: Low-to-moderate. Regulated network revenue is largely insulated from economic cycles (essential service, monopoly, cost pass-through), but growth capex/connection revenue, discretionary segments (HRV, Vector Fibre), and financing costs have some sensitivity to the broader NZ economic and construction cycle.
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: High and two-sided. Higher rates increase Vector's own finance costs on a large and growing debt book, but the DPP regulatory framework explicitly incorporates prevailing interest rates/WACC into the allowed revenue calculation at each five-year reset (DPP4 set from 1 April 2025 reflects a higher-rate environment), providing a structural, if lagged, offsetting mechanism unusual among NZX-listed companies.
macro_factors.currency_exposure: Low direct FX exposure — predominantly a NZD-denominated business; some USPP (US private placement) debt may carry hedged foreign-currency exposure, and the Bluecurrent JV has some Australian dollar exposure through its Australian metering operations.
key_input_costs: Transpower transmission charges (pass-through cost recovered via revenue, but subject to Transpower's own regulatory reset cycle)
Construction and engineering contractor costs for network build/renewal (materials, skilled labour) amid a tight NZ construction market
Debt/interest costs given the scale of the capex programme and reliance on wholesale bond, bank facility, USPP and retail bond markets
Regulatory compliance and asset management costs

recent_developments.event: FY2026 full-year results (year ended 30 June 2026) released 18 August 2026: revenue from continuing operations $1,004m (+12% YoY); adjusted EBITDA $482m (+20% YoY); NPAT $240m (+55% YoY, partly aided by absence of the prior year's $60m/$37m gas distribution impairment); EPS NZ$0.24 (up from NZ$0.15). Gross capex a record $544m (+16% YoY); net capex $353m (+36% YoY). Full-year dividend 26.00 cps (up from 25.00 cps), final dividend 13.50 cps, payout ratio ~70% (lower end of guidance band). Economic net debt $2.28bn; gearing 39% (down from the 57-59% range of FY2021-22, following the metering and gas trading sale proceeds).

FY2027 guidance issued: adjusted EBITDA $540-560m (+12-16% growth); gross capex $605-635m — a new record, reflecting record Auckland network investment including data centre connections; capital contributions guided lower at $160-190m on project timing. Management flagged a strategic review (efficiency, disciplined capital execution) to be detailed at the September 2026 shareholder/AGM meeting.

Vector confirmed a long-term Asset Management Plan (AMP26) flagging a $10 billion, 20-year investment programme in the Auckland electricity network ($4.5bn invested over the past decade; a further $5.4bn planned FY2026-FY2036), roughly half of which supports Auckland growth connections (including up to 500MW of prospective data centre demand over five years) and half supports renewal/resilience.

H1 FY2026 (six months to 31 December 2025) results: NPAT from continuing operations $113m (down ~4% YoY on a $118m base); adjusted EBITDA $240m (+19% YoY), driven by the DPP4 electricity reset (effective 1 April 2025) which lifted electricity adjusted EBITDA to $220m (+28%). Gross capex $223m (down 15% YoY in H1, guided to lift in H2). Interim dividend 12.50 cps declared. S&P credit rating reaffirmed BBB+ with (per the company's own presentation) a stable outlook. FY2026 full-year adjusted EBITDA guidance tightened to $470-490m, gross capex guidance tightened to $500-540m (from $520-590m) and capital contributions to $180-215m (from $180-230m).

Chris Blenkiron commenced as Group Chief Executive, succeeding long-serving CEO Simon Mackenzie (in the role since 2008, who led the metering and gas trading divestitures and Symphony strategy). Blenkiron previously led Rio Tinto's Tiwai Point aluminium smelter and had prior leadership roles at BlueScope in manufacturing/building products — a notable change from a utilities/networks executive background.

H1 FY2025 result (six months to 31 December 2024): NPAT from continuing operations $118m; adjusted EBITDA $202m (+16% YoY). Board approved a revised dividend policy relinking distributions to cash flow, intended to align with the Commerce Commission's five-yearly DPP regulatory cycle rather than a fixed growth trajectory. Sale of Ongas and the 60.25% Liquigas shareholding completed 31 January 2025, finalising exit from gas trading; new segment structure (electricity, gas distribution, other) adopted.

Commerce Commission published its final DPP4 (Default Price-Quality Path) determination for the 2025-2030 electricity distribution regulatory period, effective 1 April 2025, incorporating higher allowed returns reflecting the prevailing higher interest rate and inflation environment and continued pass-through of Transpower transmission costs, smoothed over the five-year period to avoid price shocks to consumers.

FY2024 annual results (year ended 30 June 2024): adjusted EBITDA from continuing operations $365.2m (+14%); NPAT (continuing operations) $79.9m, including a $60m impairment of the gas distribution business (driven by a lower regulatory return decision and higher interest rates); underlying profit excluding the impairment $139.9m. Full-year dividend 24 cps including a 1.75 cps special dividend. Gross capex $510.1m. Conditional sale of remaining gas trading businesses (Ongas, Liquigas) announced 26 July 2024 (after balance date), completing 31 January 2025.

items.notes: A new record level, up from $544m in FY2026 (+16% YoY); reflects Auckland growth, electrification and data centre connections.
Decline attributed to project timing rather than a change in underlying connection demand.

Part of a flagged $10 billion, 20-year Auckland electricity network investment programme; roughly half for growth (including up to 500MW of prospective data centre demand over 5 years), half for renewal/resilience.

prior_guidance_superseded.notes: Issued at H1 FY2026 result (Feb 2026); superseded by actual FY2026 results in Aug 2026.
Tightened down from an initial $520-590m range issued in August 2025.

guidance.management_commentary: Management (new CEO Chris Blenkiron, appointed December 2025) has emphasised record, escalating investment into the Auckland electricity network to meet growth, electrification and new large-load connections such as data centres, while flagging a strategic review focused on efficiency and disciplined capital execution to be detailed at the September 2026 shareholder meeting. The Board highlighted the favourable DPP4 regulatory reset (effective 1 April 2025) as the primary driver of the FY2026 EBITDA and NPAT step-up, and reiterated the cash-flow-linked dividend policy (revised February 2025) intended to balance shareholder distributions against the capex supercycle.

bull_case: Structural, government-sanctioned monopoly over the Auckland electricity and gas distribution networks, insulated from competitive volume loss and provided a regulated return on an expanding asset base

DPP4 reset (effective April 2025 to March 2030) has materially lifted allowable revenue and adjusted EBITDA (electricity segment EBITDA +25-28% YoY across FY26/H1FY26), reflecting the current higher interest rate/inflation environment and locking in five years of visibility

Powerful, multi-decade secular demand growth from Auckland population growth, transport/industrial electrification (EVs), and a new wave of data centre connections (up to 500MW of prospective demand flagged over five years) underpinning a $10bn, 20-year investment programme

Simplified, de-risked portfolio following the metering (FY2023, ~$1.7bn proceeds) and gas trading (FY2024) divestitures has materially reduced gearing (from 57-59% in FY2021-22 to 39% at FY2026) while retaining upside through the 50%-owned, growing Bluecurrent metering JV

Investment-grade credit rating (S&P BBB+) and demonstrated capital markets access (staggered bond/bank/USPP maturity profile through FY2036) support continued funding of the capex programme without necessarily requiring dilutive equity
bear_case: Structural capex supercycle: gross capex has persistently and increasingly exceeded operating cash flow (record $544m in FY2026, guided to a further record $605-635m in FY2027), requiring continuous new debt issuance and pushing economic net debt and gearing structurally higher over the medium term, with limited near-term visibility on when (or if) the investment programme moderates given the flagged $5.4bn plan through FY2036

Nearly all earnings power now depends on a single regulator's (Commerce Commission) five-yearly reset decisions for a single city's network — the current DPP4 settings are favourable specifically because of elevated interest rates and inflation, a tailwind that is not guaranteed to persist or repeat at the next reset (c.2030), while any adverse political intervention on consumer affordability grounds is a live risk given rising lines charges are already flowing through to Auckland household power bills

New, first-time-in-utilities CEO (Chris Blenkiron, from a mining/manufacturing background) is only months into the role and has flagged a strategic review with outcomes not yet disclosed — introducing uncertainty around capital allocation priorities, the future of the sub-scale 'Other' segment (VTS/HRV/Fibre), and continuity of the long-serving prior management team's Symphony strategy

Headline NPAT growth (+55% in FY2026) is significantly flattered by the absence of the prior year's one-off gas distribution impairment charges, and gas distribution itself faces slow structural volume decline (new connections down from 1,300 to 720 YoY in FY2026) with longer-term stranded-asset and regulatory uncertainty as NZ decarbonises

Data centre demand — a major plank of the elevated capex guidance — is inherently uncertain and subject to hyperscaler capital allocation decisions that can be delayed or downsized, creating risk that Vector's committed network investment outpaces realised connection revenue
